## Chapter 104: The Stat Menu in Minitab

### Basic Statistics

Many of the tools used to run hypothesis tests are found under Basic Statistics, in the Stat menu.

#### Descriptive and Store Descriptive Statistics

Sometimes you need to know the mean, the standard deviation, or some other descriptive statistic about your data sample. When running a lot of hypothesis tests, you need this kind of data. Minitab's Descriptive Statistics function lets you run all the most common statistics at once, and you can store them in a worksheet for reference while you work on the analysis.

*(Example data table: temperature logged over 12 time periods, ranging between 30 and 65, used for the descriptive statistics and regression examples below.)*

Copy the data above into Minitab.

Select Stat > Basic Statistics > Display Descriptive Statistics. Select the temperature column as the variable.

### Regression Analysis

Use the temperature-over-time data you copied above to run a regression analysis in Minitab. The question you want to answer is: is there a correlation between temperature and time?

Select Stat > Regression > Fitted Line Plot. Choose the temperature column as the response variable and the time column as the predictor variable.

### Statistical Tests

Most of the relevant hypothesis tests in Minitab are found under Stat > Basic Statistics or Stat > Nonparametrics.

The most relevant tests found under Stat > Basic Statistics are:

- 1 Sample Z
- 1 Sample t
- 2 Sample t
- Paired t
- 1 Proportion
- 2 Proportion
- 1 Variance
- 2 Variance
- Normality Test

**Stat → Basic Statistics** brings together: Display/Store Descriptive Statistics, Graphical Summary, 1-Sample Z, 1-Sample t, 2-Sample t, Paired t, 1 Proportion, 2 Proportions, 1-Sample/2-Sample Poisson Rate, 1/2 Variances, Correlation, Covariance, Normality Test, Outlier Test, and Goodness-of-Fit Test for Poisson.

You'll have noticed that the tests found under Basic Statistics tend to be the tests used for discrete data or normally distributed continuous data. The test for non-normally distributed continuous data can be found under Stat > Nonparametrics.

**Stat → Nonparametrics** brings together the nonparametric alternatives: 1-Sample Sign, 1-Sample Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's Median Test, Friedman, Runs Test, Pairwise Averages/Differences/Slopes — useful when the data isn't normal and t/Z tests don't apply.

### Running Hypothesis Tests

#### Example 1: 1-Proportion Test

Let's look at a few examples of hypothesis tests in Minitab. Let's revisit some of the problems discussed in the hypothesis-testing chapter.

Problem: a school administrator believes that students in a particular classroom are being affected by some environmental issue in that room. The administrator wants to check whether students in that room perform statistically worse on tests compared to students in the rest of the school; she has already observed that different class periods in that room are taught by different teachers.

The administrator collects the data. The failure rate for classes taught in any other room is 20 percent. Of 142 students who have class in that particular room, 38 are failing that specific class.

The question is: is the failure rate in that room statistically higher than the rate in other rooms? You can go back to the 1-Proportion section of chapter 48 to see how the null and alternative hypotheses are formulated.

To run the test in Minitab, select Stat > Basic Statistics > 1 Proportion. From the dropdown, select "Summarized data," since you don't have the information in columns.

The number of events is the number of occurrences you're measuring. Here, the administrator was measuring failure rates, and there were 38 failures.

The number of trials is the total number of data points. In this case, the school administrator looked at the grades of 142 students.

Check the box to perform a hypothesis test and enter the hypothesized proportion. In this case, you're comparing the classroom's actual failure rate to the overall failure rate of 20 percent. The hypothesized proportion is written as a decimal between 0 and 1.

Click Options.

Minitab generally sets the default confidence level at 95, which would set alpha at 0.05. Unless you have a specific need for higher confidence, you can leave it as is.

Select the appropriate alternative hypothesis from the dropdown. In this case, we're testing whether the proportion in our data is greater than the hypothesized proportion.

Click OK. Click OK again. Minitab displays the results, including a p-value you can use to decide whether to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis.

```
Test and CI for One Proportion

Test of p = 0.2 vs p > 0.2

Sample  X    N  Sample p  95% Lower Bound  Exact P-Value
     1  38  142  0.267606          0.207083          0.031

```

#### Example 2: 1-Sample t Test

Problem: an agricultural company that grows corn produced an average of 168 bushels of corn per acre each year, over five years. The company made a change to its seeding process, in an effort to increase the yield of its fields. The harvest after the seed change resulted in an average of 175 bushels of corn per acre each year, across 500 acres of fields. The standard deviation is 2.2 bushels. Did the seeding change result in a statistically different outcome in yield per acre?

Select Stat > Basic Statistics > 1 Sample T. Choose summarized data.

Enter the sample size, the sample mean, and the sample standard deviation from the problem. Check the box to perform a hypothesis test and enter the hypothesized mean. In this case, you want to know whether the new mean is greater than the old mean, so the old mean is the hypothesized mean.

Click OK. Click OK again.

#### Example 3: 2-Sample t Test

Copy the data from the table below into Minitab. If you recall from chapter 48, a law firm believed there was a statistical difference between how much time employees on two different teams spent on tasks.

*(Data table: minutes spent on quarter-hour tasks by 34 employees from Attorney A's team and 34 employees from Attorney B's team, with values ranging between 2 and 32 minutes.)*

Select Stat > Basic Statistics > 2-Sample T Test. From the dropdown, select that each sample is in its own column. You can also choose to analyze the samples when the data is all in a single column, or you can enter summarized data about each sample.

Select the appropriate columns in the Samples 1 and 2 boxes. In this case, you're selecting the columns containing the data for each of the teams.

Click Options.

In this case, we just want to know whether there's a difference between the two teams, so we'll leave the alternative hypothesis simply as different from the hypothesized difference. In this case, we're assuming there's no difference, so we'll leave the hypothesized difference as 0.

Click OK. Click OK again.

```
Two-Sample T-Test and CI: AttorneyA, AttorneyB

         N    Mean  StDev
AttorneyA 34  13.76   6.56
AttorneyB 34  12.82   5.07

Difference = μ (AttorneyA) - μ (AttorneyB)
Estimate for difference:  0.94
95% CI for difference:  (-1.90, 3.78)
```

Minitab displays the results, including a p-value you can use to decide whether to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis.

### The Steps for Hypothesis Tests Are Similar Across Test Types

Every hypothesis test in Minitab is run using basically the same steps as the examples above. For most test types, you can choose to test the raw data or enter summarized data. Remember, each type of hypothesis test requires different summarized data. Proportion tests require rates, mean tests generally require sample standard deviations and means, and variance tests require the sample variance. Some of the tests you might use on non-normally distributed data require the median instead of the mean.

If you have the correct descriptive statistics or have your data in columns in Minitab, it's a matter of a few clicks to set up and run a hypothesis test. The challenge isn't in running, or interpreting, the tests. It's usually in determining which test option is the right one for your data. It's worth reviewing the information in chapter 48 again to understand which types of hypothesis tests are used with different types of data and scenarios. It's also important to test your data for normality before running hypothesis tests. Remember that you can easily test for normality by running the Graphical Summary under Basic Statistics.

Other things to keep in mind when working with hypothesis tests in Minitab are that you should always click the Options button to check that your confidence interval is set appropriately and that the appropriate alternative hypothesis is selected. Minitab defaults to a 95% confidence interval and a "not equal" alternative hypothesis. However, if you're working in the same session — that is, you haven't closed Minitab since the last time you ran that specific hypothesis test — the program will remember the settings you entered and automatically apply them to the new test you're running. This can be a problem if you want to run a test on different data, or run a test on the same data with a different confidence interval or alternative hypothesis, and forget to make the change.

It's also worth noting that some of the mean tests are also found under Stat > Equivalence Test.

If you're working in Minitab and have questions about these tests, you can go to the Help menu for information on how to choose, run, and interpret each test.

Select Help > StatGuide. The topics are organized exactly like Minitab's menus. Simply select the test you want help with, and Minitab offers a dozen or more pages of help content for each one.
